claims.text: Group IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloy hydride powders are susceptible to surface oxidation and contain trapped hydrogen.
Decomposing hydride precursors in a sealed vacuum or inert environment will suppress oxygen uptake.
Hydride decomposition releases hydrogen from the precursor powder.
Immediate high-pressure extrusion or hot isostatic pressing after decomposition will densify the alloy without prolonged exposure to damaging thermal gradients.
The process requires a vacuum below 10^-3 mbar or an ultra-high-purity Ar/He atmosphere with oxygen below 1 ppm.
Hydride decomposition at 400–600 °C occurs below the onset of rapid alpha-HCP precipitation kinetics.
Consolidation should be performed at 800–1000 °C using rapid heating and followed by rapid quenching.
The proposed thermal history will retain a metastable BCC solid-solution matrix.
Low oxygen activity and rapid processing will inhibit nucleation of brittle alpha-HCP phases.
Reduced thermal input in HVAF spraying suppresses oxide formation and oxygen pickup.
High-temperature, slow-cooling regimes favor alpha-HCP precipitation, which raises the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature.
Rapid densification prevents oxygen from diffusing into the bulk alloy.
Hydrogen released during decomposition generates transient internal pressure that aids pore closure during extrusion.
The proposed hydrogen-assisted pore-closure mechanism is similar to non-equilibrium solute trapping in additive manufacturing.
The process will produce a dense bulk alloy with porosity below 0.5%.
The processed alloy will contain less than 1% alpha-HCP phase.
The processed alloy will have high-temperature yield strength comparable to or greater than conventionally processed alloys.
The proposed process will avoid catastrophic cracking.
Conventional vacuum arc melting or standard sintering of Group IV-containing HEAs typically causes significant oxygen uptake, alpha-HCP precipitation, and high porosity or cracking.
The proposed approach is limited to refractory HEAs in which Group IV elements and oxygen-driven alpha-HCP formation are the principal causes of embrittlement.

contradictions.description: The conditions prescribe 400–600 °C as a decomposition range below rapid alpha-HCP precipitation, while the uncertainty field acknowledges that the precursor-specific decomposition window is not established by the evidence.

The intervention describes solid-state hydride decomposition and hot consolidation, but the mediator invokes rapid solidification kinetics and the mechanism invokes additive-manufacturing solute trapping; no melting or solidification step is specified.
The intervention calls the environment oxygen-free, whereas the conditions permit an inert atmosphere containing up to 1 ppm oxygen; this is low-oxygen rather than strictly oxygen-free.
